nameStory: The 'fan-leaf' part of this plant's name comes from its distinctive leaves that spread out like an open hand fan, with multiple leaflets radiating from a central point. 'Chinese green dragon' refers to both its Asian origins and its unusual flower structure that resembles a hooded dragon with a long tail - a characteristic shared with other members of the arum family.
description: Fan-leaf Chinese green dragon is a small, exotic-looking perennial herb that stands about 8-12 inches tall. It produces distinctive fan-shaped leaves divided into 5-11 narrow leaflets that radiate outward like fingers from your palm. The most striking feature is its unusual greenish flower spike (called a spadix) surrounded by a hood-like bract, giving it an almost alien appearance in New England's typical woodland settings.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Hand-shaped leaves divided into 5-11 narrow, lance-shaped leaflets that feel smooth and have a waxy texture - like touching a thick magazine page

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Greenish spike surrounded by a pale green, hood-like bract that curves over the top, creating a cobra-like silhouette about 2-3 inches tall

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing plant reaching only 8-12 inches, usually producing just one or two leaves per plant from an underground bulb

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small green berries clustered along the flower spike that turn orange-red when ripe, feeling firm like tiny grapes

habitat: This rare escape from cultivation is occasionally found in disturbed woodland edges, abandoned gardens, or naturalized areas near human settlements. It prefers rich, moist soil with partial shade and is most likely to appear where someone once gardened or where garden waste was dumped.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge in late April to May, followed by the distinctive hooded flowers in May to June. This is the best time for identification when both leaves and flowers are present.
seasonality.summer: Green berries develop along the flower spike while leaves remain prominent. The fan-shaped foliage stays green and relatively fresh-looking through summer heat.
seasonality.fall: Berries ripen to orange-red and leaves begin to yellow and die back. By late fall, the above-ground parts have completely disappeared.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant underground as a bulb with no visible parts above ground, making identification impossible during this season.

funFact: Despite having only 2 recorded sightings in all of New England, this plant can multiply rapidly through tiny bulblets that form around the main bulb - meaning a single escaped plant could theoretically colonize an entire woodland edge within a few years!
confusionNotes: The fan-shaped leaf pattern is quite distinctive and unlikely to be confused with native New England plants. However, other escaped arum family members might have similar hooded flowers - look for the characteristic hand-shaped leaves with multiple narrow leaflets to confirm identification.
contextualKnowledge: **Uncertain claim**: Like many plants in the arum family, fan-leaf Chinese green dragon likely contains calcium oxalate crystals that make it toxic if eaten, causing burning sensations in the mouth and throat. This is primarily a cultivated ornamental that occasionally escapes gardens rather than a truly naturalized species in New England.
compareHints: Fan-leaf Chinese green dragon differs from its relative crowdipper by having fan-shaped leaves with 5-11 leaflets, while crowdipper has leaves divided into just three parts. Both share the characteristic arum family flower structure with a hooded bract, but the leaf shape is the easiest way to tell them apart if you're lucky enough to encounter either of these rare species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Crowdipper is the only member of the Pinellia genus commonly found in New England.
